issues.legal_issue: A government department, public undertaking, or police authority may not use adverse possession to perfect title to a citizen’s property.
material_facts: A state authority, acting through a senior police official, sued to obtain ownership of privately claimed land on the basis of adverse possession.
The private owners disputed the authority’s alleged long possession and maintained that the land had been occupied by force only recently.
Revenue records showed the property in the private owners’ names, and the lower courts rejected the state authority’s claim.
The state authority continued to challenge the adverse rulings, including by filing the special leave petition.
issues.conclusion: The special leave petition was dismissed, and the Court stated that government departments, public undertakings, and especially police departments should not be permitted to perfect title to citizens’ land or buildings by adverse possession.
issues.legal_principle: The Court treated protection of citizens’ property as a central responsibility of the State and held that state instrumentalities should not use adverse possession to take citizens’ property. It relied on the discussion of adverse possession in P.T. Munichikkanna Reddy v. Revamma and Hemaji Waghaji Jat v. Bhikhabhai Khengarbhai Harijan, including the latter’s criticism of the doctrine’s harsh effects. The Court urged Parliament to reconsider or amend the law; it did not abolish adverse possession generally.

predicates.government_entity_property_claim: A government department, public undertaking, or police authority claims a right to property.
predicates.adverse_possession_title_claim: The government entity seeks to obtain title by asserting adverse possession.
predicates.private_owner_claimant_opposed: A private citizen claims ownership of the property against the government entity.

issues.definition: When a government entity seeks title by adverse possession against a citizen who claims the property, the government entity cannot perfect title on that basis.

issues.legal_issue: A claim to ownership by adverse possession requires clear pleading and proof of possession that is open, continuous, and hostile, including when it became adverse; long possession alone is insufficient.
material_facts: The state authority alleged possession over an extended period but did not establish it with documentary evidence.
The authority did not plead when its possession became adverse or clearly plead denial of the private owners’ title.
Revenue records showed the property in the private owners’ names, and the authority’s alleged long possession was found unproved.
issues.conclusion: The state authority failed to establish adverse possession, and the courts below properly rejected its claim; the Supreme Court dismissed its special leave petition.
issues.legal_principle: A person claiming adverse possession must clearly plead and establish the facts necessary to make the possession adverse; it must be adequate in continuity, publicity, and extent, and long possession by itself is not adverse possession. The Court relied on S.M. Karim v. Mst. Bibi Sakina and on P.T. Munichikkanna Reddy v. Revamma, as discussed in Hemaji Waghaji Jat v. Bhikhabhai Khengarbhai Harijan.

predicates.adverse_possession_ownership_claim: A claimant in a property ownership proceeding asserts that possession has given the claimant title by adverse possession.
predicates.claimant_fails_to_plead_when_possession_: The claimant does not clearly state when possession became adverse to the owner’s title.
predicates.claimant_fails_to_prove_open_continuous_: The claimant does not establish possession that was open, continuous, and hostile to the owner.

issues.definition: An ownership claim by adverse possession fails when the claimant does not plead when possession became adverse and does not prove open, continuous, hostile possession.
